title: Storyworth Without Voice Recording: Writing Options (2026)
summary: Not everyone wants to be interviewed. Storyworth storytellers can answer each weekly question by email, edit any story, swap questions and keep it all private.
body_markdown:
You can picture the conversation already. You hand over the gift, explain how voice recording stories works, and you see a look of worry in their face. Some people don't want to be interviewed or aren't ready to just tell a story. They want time to reflect and remember. They want to start writing and see what comes out.


With Storyworth we make it easy for people to share in the way that's easiest for them. Whether it's voice recording or writing. Here's how our writing options work.


## Many storytellers write


A question arrives once a week by email or text. They can reply to the email directly, the same way they would reply to anyone, or write on the Storyworth site if they prefer a bigger screen.


That is the whole mechanism. No calls, no recordings, nothing to set up. For somebody who already writes emails, there is nothing new to learn.


They can add photos to any story by attaching them to the email response and they can go back and change what they wrote at any point. Nothing is locked in when they hit send.


## Nobody is watching them write


This is the reassurance worth passing on, because it is usually the real objection.


Their stories are private and owned by them forever. They decide who can see them and when. They are not posted anywhere publicly, and nobody sees a half-finished answer. The stories belong to them, and they stay available to read and edit for as long as they want them.


If they want family to see stories as they are written, they can add people to the account. If they would rather nobody read a word until the book arrives, that works too. The choice is theirs and it can change at any point.


## They do not have to answer the question they were asked


A weekly prompt is a starting point, not an assignment. There is a searchable library of questions covering childhood, education, parenthood, travel, hobbies and more. Your storyteller can swap a question they do not like, edit the wording, or write their own. They can also share a few details about their life and get questions made specifically for them.


So if the question is about their first job and what they actually want to write about is the summer they spent on their uncle’s boat, they write about the boat.


## Story length is up to them


Some questions produce three pages. Some produce two sentences. Both are fine, and the book does not look wrong either way.


This matters more than it sounds, because the fear of writing something long is what stops a lot of people from starting. Telling your mother that four sentences counts as an answer is often the thing that gets her going.


## What if other people want to contribute?


A Memoir is one person’s story, told in their words. However, if you add family members to a storyteller's account they can respond to stories with appreciation and even add memories of their own. The storyteller can decide if they want these responses added to their published memoir.


If you want to bring several people together to contribute to the same book, you can use one of our other storytelling products. Celebration Books collect stories from many people for a milestone birthday,
a retirement or an anniversary or to celebrate the life of someone who's passed. Family Newsletters bring everyone together to contribute updates to a fun monthly email.


While a plan is active, Celebrations and Family Newsletters, along with Journals are available too, so you won't need to choose between them when you purchase Storyworth.


## What to look for if you are comparing services


Most guided memoir services lean toward one answering style. Remento, Memorygram, StoryTerrace, Storii, My Life in a Book, Meminto, MyStories and Memowrite each make different assumptions about how your storyteller wants to work.


If the person you have in mind is a writer rather than a talker, three questions separate the options quickly:


1. **Can they answer by replying to an email?** Some services require you to log into
a dashboard every week, which is a small barrier that compounds over a year.
2. **Can they change the questions?** A fixed sequence works until it asks something
they do not want to answer, and then it stalls.
3. **Can they edit afterwards?** People who like writing usually like rewriting.


For a writer, the service that gets used is the one that meets them in their inbox and lets them change their mind or choose the right method for each story.
